## The model

Output is produced with a Cobb-Douglas technology, $Y = K^\alpha (AL)^{1-\alpha}$.
Labour grows at rate $n$, technology at rate $g$, capital depreciates at rate
$\delta$ and a constant fraction $s$ of output, the investment rate, is devoted to
capital accumulation.^[Textbook presentations usually call $s$ the *saving rate* and the curve $s f(k)$ *saving*. Here they are called the *investment rate* and *investment*, because what matters in the model is the proportion of output devoted to capital accumulation. The symbol $s$ is kept so that the notation matches the textbooks.]

In terms of capital per effective worker, $k = K / AL$, output is $y = k^\alpha$ and
capital evolves according to

$$
k_{t+1} = \frac{s k_t^\alpha + (1 - \delta) k_t}{(1 + n)(1 + g)} .
$$

The steady state is

$$
k^* = \left( \frac{s}{\delta + n + g + ng} \right)^{\frac{1}{1 - \alpha}} .
$$

## Simulation

Press play, or drag the time slider, to follow the economy from its initial
capital stock $k_0$. The top row shows the same $k_t$ in both charts: on the left,
the gap between investment and break-even investment is what moves $k$; on the right,
that movement is traced out over time. The remaining charts show GDP per capita,
$Y / L = A k^\alpha$, and the levels of the capital stock, $K = k A L$, and the
labour force, $L$, with $A_0 = L_0 = 1$. These keep growing after $k$ has settled
at its steady state: GDP per capita then grows at the rate of technology, $g$,
shown as a dashed line on the growth chart. On a log scale, constant growth
appears as a straight line.

See also the version with a [shock to the investment rate](shock.qmd).
